name: Concept true/false (or multiple-choice) with one-to-three-sentence justification
theory_paragraphs:
These questions sample the \term{vocabulary layer} of the whole course, so the theory to master is a set of crisp definitions. \term{CIA triad}: \term{confidentiality} = protection from unauthorized \emph{disclosure} (a read leak), \term{integrity} = protection from unauthorized \emph{modification} (output correct per specification), \term{availability} = protection from \emph{loss of use} (DoS attacks target availability). The matching threat names are \term{disclosure} (against confidentiality), \term{deception}/\term{disruption}/\term{usurpation} (against integrity --- disruption is counted as loss of integrity of service, and as a threat against availability when it blocks use entirely; on this exam, disruption was treated as an availability threat), and \term{denial of service} (against availability). \term{Privacy} is not a synonym of confidentiality: it concerns information \emph{about individuals} and includes control, context and metadata. The \term{Saltzer--Schroeder principles} are a favourite trap source and the list must be memorized \emph{exactly} --- there are eight:
\begin{tightitem}
\item \term{Least privilege}: every subject gets only the rights its task needs (fine-grained permissions).
\item \term{Fail-safe defaults}: default is deny; enumerate privileges (allowlists), not prohibitions.
\item \term{Economy of mechanism}: keep the security mechanism --- the \term{trusted computing base} (\term{TCB}), i.e.\ the small core of hardware and software whose failure would break all security --- as \emph{simple and small} as necessary (KISS).
\item \term{Complete mediation}: the reference monitor checks every operation.
\item \term{Open design} (Kerckhoffs): the attacker knows the algorithms; only the key is secret --- \imp{no security through obscurity}.
\item \term{Separation of privilege}: require collusion of two parties for a sensitive action.
\item \term{Least common mechanism}: minimize mechanisms shared by (and coupling) different users, since shared mechanisms are potential information channels.
\item \term{Psychological acceptability}: unusable security gets bypassed.
\end{tightitem}
\term{Defense in depth} (overlapping, independent layers of mechanisms) is \imp{not one of the eight} --- it is a separate doctrine, and pairing it with the Saltzer--Schroeder list is exactly the wrong-principle trap this unit trains.

Authentication and access-control facts: the three \term{authentication factors} are something you \emph{are} (biometrics), \emph{know} (password, PIN), \emph{have} (token, card); two-factor means two \emph{independent categories} --- a password plus a PIN is still one factor. \term{Authentication} itself has two parts: claiming an attribute and proving it to a verifier. \term{Salts} are random, per-user and \imp{public, non-secret}; they defeat precomputation/rainbow tables and force per-user work ($O(M\cdot N)$ instead of $O(M+N)$ for $M$ candidates and $N$ users), they do not make weak passwords strong. \term{DAC}: owner sets permissions; \term{MAC}: central authority (e.g. Bell--LaPadula). \term{ACL} = matrix column per object (easy per-object review, simple revocation, vulnerable to \term{confused deputy}); \term{capability} = unforgeable name+privilege bundle per principal (no confused deputy, but review/delegation/revocation are hard). Access control is about \term{authorization} and is meaningless unless the subject is first authenticated.

Network-security definitions: a \term{packet-filtering firewall} drops whole packets based on \emph{header metadata only} (src/dest IP and port, protocol, interface) --- it \imp{cannot filter payload content}; content filtering needs an \term{application-level gateway}/proxy or deep packet inspection, and even \term{deep packet inspection} (DPI) cannot read an \emph{end-to-end encrypted} connection --- it sees only ciphertext and metadata. A \term{stateful inspection firewall} additionally tracks the TCP connection table. IDS deployment: \term{NIDS} (on the network, cheap, transparent, but suffers inconsistent interpretation and cannot read TLS), \term{HIDS} (per host, sees what the host sees, handles encryption), log-based (cheap, no real-time). Detection styles: \term{signature-based} (blacklist of known attacks --- \imp{misses new attacks}, since a signature must be known in advance), \term{specification-based} (whitelist of allowed behaviour), \term{anomaly-based} (learned model of normal --- high false positives), \term{behavioural} (flags effects of compromise). Every detector has \term{false positives} (benign flagged) and \term{false negatives} (attacks missed); the \term{base-rate fallacy} means that with rare attacks even a tiny false-positive rate makes most alerts false alarms --- e.g.\ with a $0.01\%$ false-positive rate applied to millions of benign events, false alarms vastly outnumber the rare true attacks. DoS mechanics: \term{ICMP/UDP floods} exhaust \emph{bandwidth} (fixable only upstream --- victim-side dropping fails because \imp{the upstream link is already congested}); a \term{SYN flood} exhausts the server's \emph{pending-connection table} (state exhaustion), \imp{possible with less bandwidth than the victim}; defences are timeouts, per-IP limits and \term{SYN cookies}. \term{Reflection/amplification} abuses UDP spoofing (a 60-byte DNS query yields up to 4~KB response); \term{ingress filtering} (BCP~38) at the \emph{attacker's} ISP blocks spoofed sources.

Systems and software facts: \term{stack canaries} place a random value between locals and the saved return address and \emph{detect} its change on return --- they miss overwrites that hijack before the return or leak the canary. \term{W $\oplus$ X / NX}: data pages non-executable, blocks injected shellcode but not ROP/JOP (which reuse existing code) or data-only attacks. \term{ASLR} randomizes the layout of stack, heap and code; it fails on pointer leaks, and stack-only ASLR preserves code addresses and relative offsets. \term{Guard pages} are MMU-illegal pages that abort on any access, catching overflows and over-reads. \term{Side channels} are \emph{passive, non-invasive} observations of byproducts (time, cache, power); \term{fault injection} (e.g. electromagnetic pulses, Rowhammer) is \emph{active} and flips state --- these two are frequently swapped in traps. Malware taxonomy: a \term{virus} needs a host program and user action to spread, a \term{worm} self-propagates over the network, \term{polymorphic}/\term{encrypting} malware rewrites or re-encrypts itself so each infection looks unique, evading signatures; a \term{botnet} of hijacked machines can be rented out, e.g.\ to mine cryptocurrency for the botmaster. Web facts: the \term{SOP} isolates origins (scheme, domain, port); \term{HttpOnly} hides a cookie from JavaScript, \term{Secure} restricts it to HTTPS, \term{SameSite=Strict} sends it only same-site; parameterized queries are the correct SQLi defence. Social engineering exploits \emph{desirable} human traits (helpfulness, reciprocity, trust in authority) and works by reducing systematic thinking (time pressure, fear, altercasting) --- it is independent of the victim's intelligence, so purely technical countermeasures cannot fully stop it.
theory_cheatsheet: CIA: read leak (disclosure) = confidentiality, modification = integrity, loss of use (disruption/DoS) = availability. Privacy $>$ confidentiality (about individuals, control, metadata).

Principles (all eight): least privilege = minimum rights; fail-safe defaults = deny by default; economy of mechanism = small/simple TCB; complete mediation = check every operation; open design = attacker knows all but the key; separation of privilege = need two parties; least common mechanism = minimize shared mechanisms; psychological acceptability = usable or bypassed. Defense in depth is a separate doctrine, not on the list. Wrong-principle pairing is the classic trap.
Factors: are/know/have; 2FA = two different categories. Salt: public, per-user, defeats rainbow tables, not weak passwords. Authentication = claim + proof; access control needs authentication first.

Firewalls: packet filter = headers only, never payload; stateful = + connection table; content filtering = application proxy/DPI; DPI cannot read end-to-end encrypted traffic. SYN flood = state exhaustion (pending table, works with less bandwidth); ICMP/UDP flood = bandwidth (only upstream/ISP can fix; ingress filtering kills spoofing).

IDS: signature detects only known attacks; anomaly = learned normal, many false positives; every detector has FP and FN; base-rate fallacy: rare attacks $\Rightarrow$ even a tiny FP rate floods you with false alarms.

Defences' limits: canary detects return-address overwrite only; NX blocks injected code, not ROP/JOP; ASLR fails on leaks. Side channel = passive observation; fault injection = active. Virus needs host+user action; worm self-propagates.
identify_givens: A battery of short standalone statements (typically 5--6 for the E-level Part~1), each making one claim about a security concept, mechanism or attack --- e.g.\ equating two notions (``Privacy is a synonym for confidentiality''), attributing a mechanism (``A packet filtering firewall filters out specific content''), mis-mapping threats to CIA properties, or naming a design principle (``\ldots goes against the principle of economy of mechanism''). Variants: (a) a Canvas-style quiz where each statement is answered True/False with feedback, and (b) multiple-choice options A--D marked with the club symbol where zero, one or several options may be true and ``None of these answers are correct'' is offered.
identify_target: For each statement, decide true/false (or mark all true options) and justify the verdict in one to three sentences by naming the correct property, definition or principle and giving the key distinction or counterexample. Grading typically awards the point if the reasoning makes at least one of the listed correct points.
identify_keywords: classify them as true or false and explain your reasoning
None of these answers are correct
strategy_name: Name the concept, then give the distinguishing counterexample

algorithm.detail: Write down (mentally) the precise course definition of that concept, e.g.\ packet-filtering firewall = drop whole packets based on header metadata only, never payload; economy of mechanism = the security mechanism should not be more complex than necessary; anomaly-based IDS = learned model of normal behaviour, hence high false positives; SYN flood = exhaustion of the pending-connection table.

Check the usual mismatch patterns:
\begin{tightitem}
\item absolute quantifiers (``only'', ``all'', ``never'', ``necessarily''),
\item claimed synonyms between notions of different scope (privacy vs.\ confidentiality),
\item swapped CIA properties (a read violation is confidentiality, not integrity; disruption is availability),
\item a real bad practice paired with the \term{wrong named principle} (or a non-principle like defense in depth presented as one of the eight Saltzer--Schroeder principles),
\item a mechanism attributed to the wrong layer (content filtering needs DPI, not packet filtering) or wrong resource (SYN flood exhausts state, not bandwidth).
\end{tightitem}

Mark \emph{true} only if the statement is correct as written, including the named principle and quantifiers; a statement whose underlying observation is right but whose justification names the wrong principle is \emph{false}. For club-marked multiple choice, judge each option A--D \term{independently} --- several (or none) may be true, and never select ``None of these answers are correct'' together with another option.

In 1--3 sentences: state the verdict, give the correct definition, and name the distinguishing counterexample or correction, e.g.\ ``False: students only need read access to most pages, so this violates \term{least privilege}; economy of mechanism means the mechanism should not be more complex than necessary.'' \imp{Aim to hit at least one of the grading scheme's accepted points} --- give the sharpest distinction, not an essay.

variations.name: Single T/F battery with reasoning (2022 style)
variations.detail: Six independent statements, each classified and justified; grading accepts any one of several listed correct points. Trap: some statements are false because of the \term{mechanism or principle named}, not because the intuition is wrong --- so always check the justification clause, not just the headline claim.

variations.name: Canvas quiz T/F with feedback (dasak20/dasak21 style)
variations.detail: The same statements appear as an online quiz with True/False radio buttons; official feedback explains the verdict. The style is identical to the written battery: e.g.\ threat-to-CIA mapping (``disclosure and disruption are threats against integrity'' --- False), base-rate fallacy (``$0.01\%$ false positives, yet overwhelmed by false alarms, so the vendor lied'' --- False). Prepare by memorizing the distinguishing correction for each classic trap.

variations.name: Multiple-true club format (dasak19 Part I)
variations.detail: Options A--D under a topic header (Concepts/CIA, Authentication, Cryptography, Memory safety, Malware, IDS/Firewalls) are graded \term{independently}; zero, one or several may be true. E.g.\ on IDS/firewalls all of these are true: signature IDS detects only known intrusions, firewalls do not stop internal threats, detection necessarily has false positives/negatives. ``None of these answers are correct'' exists to separate ``all false'' from ``unanswered''.

variations.name: Wrong-principle pairing / synonym-quantifier trap
variations.detail: The statement describes a genuine security mistake but attributes it to the wrong Saltzer--Schroeder principle (economy of mechanism instead of least privilege, or vice versa) --- or invokes a principle that is not in the canonical eight at all. Similarly, words like ``synonym'', ``only'', ``necessarily'', ``never'' make a roughly-true statement false: privacy is broader than confidentiality; message authentication does \emph{not} require encrypting the content; a MAC gives integrity and \imp{no confidentiality}. Verify the named principle's definition against the exact list and test edge cases against the quantifier.

walkthrough_problem: Part 1, true/false with reasoning: ``A company replaces its signature-based IDS with an anomaly-based IDS and configures its new deep-packet-inspection firewall to read the content of TLS-encrypted web sessions, so that both previously unseen attacks can be detected with few false positives and malicious payloads inside encrypted traffic can be filtered at the perimeter.'' Classify the statement as true or false and explain your reasoning.

walkthrough_steps.work: First, slow down and split the statement into its individual claims --- a single sentence here contains \emph{two} linked assertions: (a) an \term{anomaly-based IDS} detects previously unseen attacks \emph{with few false positives}, and (b) a \term{deep-packet-inspection (DPI) firewall} can read the \emph{content} of TLS-encrypted traffic. Beginner pitfall: judging the sentence as a whole because it ``sounds reasonable''. Each clause must be checked on its own; one wrong clause makes the whole statement false.

Recall the exact definitions. An \term{anomaly-based IDS} learns a model of what \emph{normal} looks like and flags anything that deviates. Yes, this catches novel attacks (a signature IDS cannot --- its patterns must be known in advance), but the price is a \emph{high} false-positive rate: unusual-but-legitimate behaviour is flagged too. \term{TLS} encrypts the payload end-to-end between client and server, so any middlebox sees only ciphertext and header metadata; reading the plaintext content is \imp{impossible without terminating the TLS session} (an interception proxy) or watching at the endpoint (a HIDS).

Now hunt the traps. Clause (a) swaps the signature/anomaly trade-off: novelty detection is \emph{bought at the cost of} false positives, so ``few false positives'' directly contradicts the definition --- and the \term{base-rate fallacy} makes it even worse when attacks are rare. Clause (b) attributes plaintext visibility on \emph{encrypted} traffic to a network middlebox: a plain DPI firewall does not break TLS. Why a beginner misses this: both clauses state a real \emph{advantage} (novel detection; DPI does inspect payloads of unencrypted traffic) and quietly overstate it. The exam loves overstatements.

Verdict: \textbf{False}. Both the stated detection benefit (``few false positives'') and the stated firewall capability (reading TLS content) are wrong as written. Note that you do not need to fix the statement --- just to classify it. But being able to say \emph{what would be true} (``detects novel attacks but with many false positives''; ``can filter only unencrypted payloads'') is exactly what earns the reasoning point.

Justification to write (1--3 sentences, verdict first): ``False. An \term{anomaly-based IDS} can detect previously unseen attacks, but its learned model of normality produces \emph{high} false-positive rates, and the base-rate fallacy amplifies this for rare attacks. A DPI firewall cannot read TLS content: the payload is end-to-end encrypted, so only ciphertext and header metadata are visible --- plaintext inspection requires terminating the TLS session (interception proxy) or endpoint visibility such as a \term{HIDS}.'' Common mistake to avoid: writing a whole essay about IDS types without ever stating the verdict or the single sharpest distinction.

exam_questions.problem: ``Disclosure and disruption are examples of threats against integrity.'' True or false?

solution_steps.work: Isolate the claim: this is a \term{threat-to-CIA mapping} question. It asserts that \emph{both} named threats --- \term{disclosure} and \term{disruption} --- belong to the same CIA property, integrity. Beginner note: each threat name has exactly one canonical CIA property in this course, so the statement is really two mini-claims fused together.

Recall the definitions: \term{confidentiality} is protection against unauthorized \emph{reading} of data --- a \term{disclosure} is precisely such a read leak, so disclosure is a threat against \emph{confidentiality}. \term{Integrity} is protection against unauthorized \emph{modification}. \term{Availability} is protection against loss of use --- a \term{disruption} interrupts or degrades service, so disruption is a threat against \emph{availability}.

Hunt the trap: this is the classic \term{swapped CIA properties} pattern. Both threat words are placed under the wrong heading; neither belongs to integrity. A beginner mistake is to reason ``disruption damages the system, and damage sounds like integrity'' --- but the course definition of integrity is about \emph{unauthorized modification of data/output}, not about service being up or down.
Verdict: \textbf{False} --- the mapping is wrong for both threats.

Official feedback (write something equivalent): ``The statement is FALSE: disclosure is a threat against \term{confidentiality}, disruption is a threat against \term{availability}.'' One sentence suffices --- verdict plus the two correct mappings.

exam_questions.answer: False --- disclosure threatens confidentiality; disruption threatens availability.

exam_questions.problem: ``Your company bought the best intrusion detection system on the market. It has only 0.01\% false positives. However, your company is overwhelmed with false alarms, so the manufacturer must have lied about the false-positive rate in their marketing material.'' True or false?

solution_steps.work: Isolate the claim: this tests the \term{base-rate fallacy} for intrusion detection. The logic offered is: many false alarms observed $\Rightarrow$ the advertised false-positive rate must be a lie. Beginner note: a \term{false-positive rate} is the probability that a \emph{benign} event is flagged; it says nothing directly about how \emph{many} alarms you will see in total.

Recall the definitions: a \term{false positive} is a benign event incorrectly flagged as an attack. The total number of false alarms equals the false-positive rate \emph{multiplied by the number of benign events}. If benign events vastly outnumber real attacks (the attack base rate is tiny), even a very small rate yields a flood of false alarms.

Hunt the trap: the statement commits the \term{base-rate fallacy} --- it ignores the base rate of real attacks. Concretely: with millions of benign events per day, $0.01\%$ of them is still hundreds of false alarms daily, while genuine attacks may be only a handful. So a truthful manufacturer and an overwhelming alarm load are \emph{perfectly compatible}; the conclusion ``must have lied'' does not follow.

Official feedback (write something equivalent): ``Yes, indeed (the statement is false). This can happen even with a very low false-positive rate like that. If the number of true positive cases is much smaller than the number of true negative cases, then those $0.01\%$ of false positives can grow very large.'' The key phrase to include is the comparison between the \emph{rare} attacks and the \emph{huge} mass of benign events.

exam_questions.answer: False --- with rare attacks, even a 0.01% false-positive rate over a huge volume of benign events produces overwhelming false alarms (base-rate fallacy).

exam_questions.source: Partial Exam October 2022, Part 1, T/F statement 5
exam_questions.problem: ``Allowing students write access to all canvas pages in a course goes against the principle of economy of mechanism.'' Classify the statement as true or false and explain your reasoning.

solution_steps.work: Isolate the claim: this is a \term{wrong-principle pairing} question. It describes a real access-control mistake (students get \emph{write} access to \emph{all} pages) and asserts it violates a specific named Saltzer--Schroeder principle: \term{economy of mechanism}. Two things must \emph{both} be right for True: that the practice is bad, and that the \emph{named principle} is the one it violates.

Recall the definitions: \term{economy of mechanism} says the security mechanism (the TCB) should be as \emph{simple and small} as necessary --- it is about \emph{design complexity}, not about who gets which rights. \term{Least privilege} says every subject should get only the rights its task actually needs.

Hunt the trap: the intuition ``students should not be able to write everywhere'' is correct --- but the principle that forbids it is \term{least privilege} (students only need \emph{read} access to most pages, unless a specific task requires writing), not economy of mechanism. Beginner mistake: marking True because ``the practice described is indeed bad''. The verdict follows the \emph{pairing}, not the practice.

Official solution (either accepted point suffices; write both to be safe): ``False. 1) It goes against the principle of \term{least privilege}, as students only need read access to most pages unless a task requires them to write. 2) \term{Economy of mechanism} means that a security mechanism should not be more complex than necessary.'' Note the grading hint: ``correct reasoning makes at least one of these points'' --- so naming the correct principle alone already scores.

exam_questions.answer: False --- the practice violates least privilege, not economy of mechanism (which is about keeping the mechanism simple).
